stages.title: Reading and writing fundamentals
stages.hook: Read the word كتاب with no vowel marks. How do you know it is "kitāb" and not "kutub"?
explain: Arabic letters mainly write consonants. Long vowels are written with ا (ā), ي (ī) and و (ū). Short vowels are small marks: fatḥa (a), kasra (i), ḍamma (u). A sukūn means no vowel, a shadda doubles a consonant, and tanwīn gives the endings -an, -in, -un.
Adults normally read without short vowels, because they know the words. Children's books, the Qur'an and learner books add the marks. To read unmarked text you need vocabulary and the context.
When letters join, the word looks like one flowing shape: ك + ت + ا + ب gives كتاب. Hamza (ء) is a glottal stop and sits on ا, و, ي or by itself.
stages.mnemonic: Three tiny marks, three short vowels: a above, u above-curl, i below.
sentences: The school is near the house.

gq.why: Sukūn marks that the consonant has no short vowel after it.
Shadda marks gemination, as in madrasa (the "s" is single) versus muʿallim (the "l" is doubled).

panel.q: Why can an adult read a newspaper without short vowels?
o: Context and vocabulary tell which word it is
panel.why: Skilled readers know the word patterns and use context to supply the vowels.

panel.q: What is the main reason the Qur'an and children's books are fully vowelled?
o: To show the exact reading and help learners
panel.why: Full harakat remove ambiguity and teach correct reading.

panel.q: Why does the unvowelled word كتب have more than one possible reading?
panel.model: Without short vowels the same letters can be kataba (he wrote), kutub (books) or kutiba (it was written), so context decides.
panel.why: Short vowels are not written, so different words can share one spelling.

teach.topic: Reading Arabic with and without vowels
teach.model: Arabic writes mostly consonants. Small marks above or below show short vowels. Books for adults usually leave them out, but learner books add them.

points.ask: What do the letters mainly show?
What shows the short vowels?
How do adults read without marks?

stages.title: Basic sentence construction
stages.hook: In English we say "The house is big". In Arabic we simply say "The house big". Where did the word "is" go?
explain: Arabic has two main sentence types. A nominal sentence starts with a noun: al-baytu kabīr, "the house is big". There is no word for "is" in the present. A verbal sentence starts with a verb: yaktubu aṭ-ṭālibu, "the student writes".
In a nominal sentence the first part is the subject (mubtadaʾ) and the second the predicate (khabar). The predicate agrees in gender and number: al-bint dhakiyya (the girl is clever), al-walad dhakī.

When the verb comes first, it stays singular even if the subject is plural: yaktubu aṭ-ṭullāb, "the students write". In this course we omit the final case endings of nouns for easier reading, as many speakers do in speech.
stages.mnemonic: No "is" needed: just put the two parts side by side, like two blocks.
items: the book is on the table
the teacher is in the class
sentences: The house is big and new.
My brother is a skilled doctor.

gq.q: How do you say "the house is big" in Arabic?
gq.why: The present "is" is left out: noun plus predicate.

gq.q: In yaktubu aṭ-ṭullāb ("the students write"), why is the verb singular?
o: A verb that comes first stays singular
Plural verbs are only for writing
gq.why: In verb-first sentences the verb agrees in gender but stays singular.

panel.q: What is the difference between al-bayt al-kabīr and al-bayt kabīr?
o: The first is a phrase "the big house", the second a sentence "the house is big"
panel.why: With al- on both words it is a noun phrase; with al- only on the noun it becomes a complete sentence.

panel.q: Why is dhakiyya used with al-bint but dhakī with al-walad?
o: The predicate adjective agrees in gender with the subject
panel.why: Arabic adjectives agree in gender.

panel.q: Which is the verbal sentence?
panel.why: A verbal sentence begins with a verb.

teach.model: A nominal sentence begins with a noun and has no word for is, like al-bayt kabīr. A verbal sentence begins with a verb, like yaqraʾ aṭ-ṭālib al-kitāb.

points.ask: Is there a word for is?
What starts a verbal sentence?
Can you show me a nominal sentence?

stages.title: Common verbs
stages.hook: "I went", "you went", "she went": in Arabic, the end of one verb word tells you who. Can you spot the clue?
explain: Arabic past verbs use endings for the person. The base form is the "he" form: kataba (he wrote). Add -tu for I (katabtu), -ta for you (m) (katabta), -ti for you (f) (katabti), -at for she (katabat), -nā for we (katabnā).

This means pronouns are not needed: ذَهَبْتُ (dhahabtu) already means "I went". The same root gives present (yadhhab) and past (dhahaba) forms. Common past verbs: kataba (wrote), dhahaba (went), akala (ate), shariba (drank), fataḥa (opened), jalasa (sat), samiʿa (heard), raʾā (saw).
Say a verb aloud and listen to the ending. The last vowel often tells you the person.
stages.mnemonic: -tu ends "I" (katabtu), -ta ends "you" (katabta): the ending is the pronoun.
sentences: We opened the window in the morning.

gq.q: Which ending means "I" in the past tense?
What is the "he" past form of the root k-t-b?
gq.why: Kataba (he wrote) is the base past form.

panel.q: Why is the pronoun often dropped in ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة?
o: The verb ending already shows the speaker is "I"
panel.why: Arabic verb endings carry person, gender and number.

panel.q: How do you tell katabta (you, m) from katabti (you, f)?
panel.why: The final short vowel shows the gender of "you".

panel.q: "Katabat Sara" means "Sara wrote". Why is it katabat and not kataba?
o: Sara is feminine, so the verb takes -at
panel.why: The verb agrees in gender with its subject.

teach.model: Arabic past verbs have endings for the person: -tu for I, -ta for you and -at for she. The pronoun is often not needed.

points.ask: How does the verb show who did it?
Do I need I or you?
Can you give an example?

stages.title: Nouns, pronouns and modifiers
stages.hook: "Teacher" is muʿallim for a man. What do you think changes for a woman?
explain: Personal pronouns: anā (I), anta (you, m), anti (you, f), huwa (he), hiya (she), naḥnu (we), antum (you, pl m), hum (they, m). Arabic also has a dual (two people) form, which most beginners learn later.

Nouns are masculine or feminine. Feminine is often marked with ـة: muʿallim (male teacher), muʿallima (female teacher). Plurals are either "sound" (muʿallimūn, muʿallimāt) or "broken" (kitāb → kutub, walad → awlād), where the inside of the word changes.
Adjectives agree with nouns in gender, number and definiteness. After a definite noun the adjective also takes al-: al-bayt al-kabīr (the big house).
stages.mnemonic: Broken plural: the word breaks and rebuilds inside, like kitāb → kutub.

gq.q: What is the plural of kitāb (book)?
How do you say "the big house" in Arabic?
gq.why: Both the noun and adjective take al- and the adjective follows.

panel.q: Why is "al-bayt al-kabīr" a phrase but "al-bayt kabīr" a sentence?
o: Matching al- on both makes a phrase; only the noun definite makes a statement
panel.why: The definiteness of the adjective decides if it describes (phrase) or states (sentence).

panel.q: Which plural is "sound feminine" for muʿallima?
panel.why: Sound feminine plural adds -āt.

panel.q: Explain what a broken plural is, with an example.
panel.model: A broken plural changes the inside pattern of the word instead of adding an ending, for example kitāb (book) becomes kutub (books) and walad (boy) becomes awlād (boys).
panel.why: Many common Arabic nouns form plurals by changing the internal vowel and letter pattern.

teach.model: Arabic has pronouns like anā for I and huwa for he. Nouns have gender. Plurals can add an ending, or the word changes inside, like kitāb to kutub.

points.ask: What are the pronouns?
Do nouns have gender?
How does a plural form?

stages.title: Questions and responses
stages.hook: To ask a yes/no question in Arabic, add a tiny word at the start. Guess which word asks "Do you speak Arabic?"
explain: Yes/no questions start with hal: hal tatakallamu al-ʿarabiyya? "Do you speak Arabic?" The answers are naʿam (yes) and lā (no). In writing, the question mark is turned backwards: ؟.
Question words are: man (who), mā (what), ayna (where), matā (when), kayfa (how), limādhā (why), kam (how many). So ayna al-madrasa? means "where is the school?".
Dialects change the question words: "why" is limādhā in MSA, laysh in the Levant, leh in Egypt, and leysh in the Gulf. Use MSA in formal speech and writing.
stages.mnemonic: Hal opens the door for yes or no; the question words open the door for information.

gq.q: Which word starts a yes/no question?
In Egyptian Arabic, "why" is often "leh". In MSA it is:

panel.q: A learner replies to "hal anta ṭālib?" with "ayna". Why is this a mismatch?
o: Hal asks yes/no, so the answer should be naʿam or lā
panel.why: A yes/no question needs naʿam or lā.

panel.q: Where does a question word such as ayna or limādhā normally go in an MSA question?
o: At the start of the sentence
At the end of the sentence
Between the verb and the subject
Nowhere: it is replaced by a rising voice
panel.why: Question words open the sentence in MSA.

panel.q: Why is the question mark ؟ backwards?
o: It mirrors the right-to-left direction of writing
It is only used in poetry
panel.why: Punctuation in Arabic is adapted to the right-to-left direction.

teach.model: For yes or no, begin with hal. For information use words like mā for what, ayna for where and limādhā for why.

points.ask: How do I ask a yes or no question?
What are the other question words?
Do all Arabs use the same words?

stages.title: Describing people and places
stages.hook: Describe a friend: tall? kind? funny? In Arabic, the describing word comes after the person. Why might that help the listener?
explain: Descriptions use adjectives after the noun: al-walad aṭ-ṭawīl, the tall boy. For a girl: al-bint aṭ-ṭawīla. Add ـة for feminine: laṭīf → laṭīfa (kind).
Plural adjectives for people often follow the noun as well: awlād ṭiwāl. For things, a plural noun takes a feminine singular adjective: kutub jadīda (new books). This is a classic feature of Arabic.
To compare, use the pattern aCCaC: kabīr becomes akbar (bigger), jamīl becomes ajmal (more beautiful). "Bigger than" is akbar min.
stages.mnemonic: Things in a crowd are one feminine group: kutub jadīda.
sentences: The city is big and beautiful.
My teacher is kind and clever.
The park is near my house.

gq.q: How do you say "new books" in MSA?
gq.why: Plural things take a feminine singular adjective: kutub jadīda.
The aCCaC pattern with min gives the comparative.

panel.q: Why is "al-madīna kabīra" feminine?
panel.why: Adjectives agree with the noun.

panel.q: Which phrase means "the most beautiful city"?
panel.why: The superlative uses aCCaC before a singular noun.

panel.q: Where does the adjective go in Arabic, and what must it match?
panel.model: It comes after the noun and agrees with it in gender, number and definiteness.
panel.why: Arabic adjectives follow the noun and agree with it.

teach.model: An Arabic adjective comes after the noun and agrees with it. Add a feminine ending for a feminine noun. A plural thing takes a feminine singular adjective.

points.ask: Where does the adjective go?
What must it match?
Is there anything surprising about plurals?

stages.title: Time, dates and daily routines
stages.hook: Which day of the week do many Muslims gather for the midday prayer? In many Arab countries, that day is part of the weekend. Which one?
explain: Days of the week in Arabic: al-aḥad (Sunday), al-ithnayn (Monday), ath-thulāthāʾ (Tuesday), al-arbiʿāʾ (Wednesday), al-khamīs (Thursday), al-jumʿa (Friday), as-sabt (Saturday). Their names come from numbers: aḥad means one, ithnayn two.

The weekend varies by country: many use Friday and Saturday, while a few use Saturday and Sunday. For the future, put sa- before a present verb: sa-nusāfiru, "we will travel". Besides the Gregorian calendar, the Islamic (Hijri) lunar calendar is used for religious dates.

Daily routines use present verbs: astayqiẓu (I wake up), aghtasilu (I wash), aʾkulu al-iftār (I eat breakfast), adhhab ilā al-madrasa. For time use as-sāʿa (the hour/clock): as-sāʿa as-sābiʿa is seven o'clock.
stages.mnemonic: Aḥad = one, ithnayn = two: the week counts itself.
sentences: I wake up at seven o'clock.
Tomorrow we will travel to Cairo.

gq.q: Which Arabic day name literally means "one"?
What is the Islamic calendar based on?
gq.why: The Hijri calendar is lunar, with months of 29 or 30 days.

panel.q: Why do Arab countries not all share the same weekend?
o: Each country sets its own working week
panel.why: The weekend is a national decision and has changed over time.

panel.q: Why can sa-/sawfa before a verb show the future?
panel.why: Sa- + present verb gives the future.

panel.q: Why is ghadan (tomorrow) not changed for gender?
panel.model: Ghadan is an adverb of time. Adverbs do not agree with gender or number.
panel.why: Adverbs like ghadan and al-yawm stay the same.

teach.model: Days of the week are al-aḥad (one), al-ithnayn (two) and so on up to al-jumʿa and as-sabt. The Islamic calendar is lunar. For routines use present verbs.

points.ask: Where do the day names come from?
What is the Islamic calendar?
How do I say what I do each day?

stages.title: Food and shopping
stages.hook: In a market in Cairo or Marrakesh people may bargain. What polite question starts any purchase?
explain: To ask the price say bikam hādhā? "how much is this?" or kam siʿruhu? In the Levant, people say "bikam" too, and in Egypt "bekām". For quantities use a measure word and the noun: kūb shāy, a cup of tea.

Food words: aruzz (rice), dajāj (chicken), laḥm (meat), tuffāḥ (apples), shāy (tea), qahwa (coffee). Arabic coffee, dates and olive oil are part of hospitality in many countries. Offering tea or coffee to a guest is a normal sign of welcome.
To ask for something say urīd ... (I want ...) or min faḍlik, aʿṭinī ... (please give me ...). Reply to a seller with ghālī (expensive) or rakhīṣ (cheap) when you talk about price.
stages.mnemonic: Bikam? = "by how much?": the first word in any shop.
sentences: I would like a cup of tea.
The coffee is hot and delicious.

panel.q: Why is "tea" shāy usually a "cup of tea" (kūb shāy) in the shop?
o: Quantities are expressed with a measure word followed by the noun
Arabic has no word for cup
panel.why: A measure word plus noun is the normal pattern for quantities.

panel.q: Which reply to a seller is polite when you think the price is too high?
panel.why: Saying it is a little expensive is polite and starts bargaining.

panel.q: Why is saying "urīd" to a seller still polite if you add min faḍlik?
panel.why: Adding min faḍlik adds politeness.

teach.model: Say bikam hādhā to ask how much. Say urīd to say what you want. Add min faḍlik to be polite.

points.ask: How do I ask the price?
How do I say what I want?
How do I stay polite?

stages.title: Everyday conversations
stages.hook: You meet someone new and want to chat. What three questions could you ask first?
explain: A simple conversation: Mā ismuka? (What is your name?) – Ismī Karīm. Min ayna anta? (Where are you from?) – Anā min al-Maghrib (Morocco). Tasharrafnā means "we are honoured", a polite way to say "nice to meet you".

When you are asked "How are you?", the usual answer is bi-khayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh (fine, thanks to God). "Inshāʾ Allāh" (God willing) is often added when you talk about the future. These phrases are common in every Arab country, in MSA and dialect.

Arabic speakers often welcome you with ahlan wa sahlan; the reply is ahlan bik. In real life many people mix MSA and dialect. If a dialect word is used, name the dialect: for example, "izzayyak" is Egyptian.
stages.mnemonic: Ahlan wa sahlan: "family and ease": you are with family here.
items: what is your name? (to a man)
where are you from? (to a man)
sentences: We will meet tomorrow, God willing.

gq.q: What is the usual answer to kayfa ḥāluk?
gq.why: You answer that you are well and give thanks.

panel.q: Why is "izzayyak" not suitable for a formal speech?
o: It is Egyptian dialect, while formal speech uses MSA
panel.why: Dialect belongs to everyday talk.

panel.q: What does adding "in shāʾ Allāh" to a plan say?
o: The plan is hoped for with God's will; it is also a common polite habit
The speaker is unsure and does not want to go
panel.why: It reflects a cultural habit of humility about the future.

panel.q: Why is it useful to know both MSA and one dialect?
panel.model: MSA is understood across the Arab world and used in writing and news. A dialect is used for everyday talk with friends and family.
panel.why: Arabic is diglossic: formal MSA and local dialects are used for different purposes.

teach.model: Ask mā ismuka for the name and min ayna anta for where you are from. Answer bi-khayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh when someone asks how you are. Add in shāʾ Allāh when talking about the future.

points.ask: How do I ask someone's name?
How do I ask where they are from?
What do I say when asked how I am?
